profile.campus: Not part of Iron Mountain's marketed CHI-1 data-center campus (Des Plaines, IL); City of Chicago building-permit records identify this address as a records-storage warehouse
profile.reading:
Iron Mountain Incorporated (NYSE: IRM) is a publicly traded REIT headquartered in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. The company has two distinct lines of business relevant here: a decades-old, much larger physical and digital records-management segment operated out of warehouse-type facilities nationally, and a newer data center REIT segment built substantially through a January 2018 acquisition of IO Data Centers, spanning more than 30 marketed locations globally.

Iron Mountain's own data center site lists exactly one Chicago-area IT facility, internally designated CHI-1, at 1680 Touhy Avenue, Des Plaines, Illinois, roughly 13 miles from this address: 315,000 square feet on a 13-acre campus, with a 36 MW IT design capacity (56 MW total facility capacity), per the operator's own page. This registry's "2421-2425 S Halsted St, Chicago" entry does not correspond to that facility.

Public City of Chicago building-permit records list Iron Mountain as owner at 2421 and 2425 South Halsted Street, in the Bridgeport neighborhood near the former Union Stock Yards, with permits covering a 106,000 square-foot roof repair (2010) and the installation of vertical reciprocating conveyor lifts inside an existing "storage facility" (2011). That permit language, and the absence of this address from Iron Mountain's own marketed data center portfolio, indicates this is a physical records-storage warehouse rather than a colocation data center; this registry records that determination honestly rather than asserting IT capacity or square footage figures that were not found. Readers researching Iron Mountain's actual Chicago-area data center capacity should look to CHI-1 in Des Plaines instead, which is not currently tracked as a separate row in this registry.

Iron Mountain trades on the New York Stock Exchange under ticker IRM and files with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission under CIK 0001020569, structured as a real estate investment trust. Records management remains the company's larger, founding business line by facility count nationally; the Bridgeport-area Halsted Street building sits in a historically industrial corridor near the former Union Stock Yards, a district that has long hosted warehouse and logistics operations of exactly this kind rather than modern colocation infrastructure.
profile.capacity_note: No IT capacity, tier certification, or data-center-specific specs found. City of Chicago building permit records (owner listed as Iron Mountain) show roof repair and vertical-lift/conveyor installation work at this address, characteristic of a warehouse rather than IT infrastructure buildout (no generator, chiller, UPS, or raised-floor permits found).
profile.research_note: Gap-view review: City of Chicago building-permit records at 2421-2425 S Halsted St describe a "storage facility" (roof repair, conveyor lift installation), and this address does not appear in Iron Mountain's marketed data center portfolio (which lists only CHI-1 in Des Plaines for the Chicago area). This is a physical records-storage warehouse, not a colocation data center; no IT capacity or technical square footage figure exists to write. Readers should look to CHI-1 (Des Plaines) for Iron Mountain's actual Chicago-area data center capacity.

reading.body:
Iron Mountain operates a 36 MW data center in Chicago with carrier-neutral connectivity and N plus 1 redundancy, though the company does not publish specific capacity details for the facility.

Iron Mountain built its data center business through acquisition rather than construction. The company purchased IO Data Centers' United States division in 2017 for 1.3 billion dollars, gaining four colocation facilities in New Jersey, Ohio, and Arizona. This Chicago location may or may not have been part of that transaction. The operator's own current locations page confirms Chicago as an active market without disclosing the street address.

For AI workloads, carrier-neutral colocation facilities differ from hyperscaler-owned data centers. A carrier-neutral facility can serve multiple operators and network providers rather than one company's internal compute demand. This matters for AI scaling only if the facility's power supply, cooling capacity, and network connections can absorb the electrical and bandwidth requirements of dense GPU clusters, data Iron Mountain's public listing does not detail.

The available data does not cover power consumption, cooling type, GPU adoption, or whether this facility actually hosts AI training or inference workloads. It confirms a real facility and its nominal IT capacity. It does not establish whether that capacity is spoken for, or whether it represents a binding constraint on AI compute in Chicago or the broader Midwest.
